Speechless
spēch´lĕs
adj. (unable to speak; in the parables and in Acts, the silence of a man with nothing to say for himself)
English speech + -less. The Greek of Matthew 22 is phimoo, to be muzzled — the same verb Christ used to still the sea and to silence the unclean spirit.

Biblical Definition

Three silences. At the wedding the king finds a man without a garment: “Friend, how camest thou in hither not having a wedding garment? And he was speechless” (Mat 22:12), and the sentence follows at once (Mat 22:13). Zacharias, who had doubted Gabriel, “could not speak unto them… for he beckoned unto them, and remained speechless” (Luk 1:22), having been told, “thou shalt be dumb, and not able to speak… because thou believest not my words” (Luk 1:20). And on the Damascus road, “the men which journeyed with him stood speechless, hearing a voice, but seeing no man” (Act 9:7).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines speechless as destitute or deprived of the power of speaking, and also as mute or silent, not speaking for a time.

expand to see more

SPEECHLESS, a. Destitute or deprived of the faculty of speech.

SPEECHLESS, a. Mute; silent; not speaking for a time.

MUZZLE, v.t. To bind the mouth; to fasten the mouth to prevent biting or eating.

Key Scripture

Mat 22:12 — "And he saith unto him, Friend, how camest thou in hither not having a wedding garment? And he was speechless."

Mat 22:13 — "Then said the king to the servants, Bind him hand and foot, and take him away, and cast him into outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth."

Luk 1:20 — "And, behold, thou shalt be dumb, and not able to speak, until the day that these things shall be performed, because thou believest not my words, which shall be fulfilled in their season."

Rom 3:19 — "Now we know that what things soever the law saith, it saith to them who are under the law: that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God."

Modern Corruption

The man without the wedding garment had no answer, and Scripture makes that silence the posture of every sinner before the law.

expand to see more

Matthew 22:12 and Romans 3:19 are the same doctrine in two keys. The guest is inside the hall, seated, apparently accepted, and one question undoes him: how camest thou in hither not having a wedding garment? He was speechless — muzzled, the Greek says, the word used of the silenced sea. Paul states the principle: the law speaks that every mouth may be stopped and all the world become guilty before God. Justification cannot begin until the excuses end, and the whole doctrine of imputed righteousness stands on the fact that the garment is provided rather than produced. He was not cast out for lacking merit; he was cast out for coming in his own.

The corruption to name is the confidence that a reasonable account of oneself will be accepted at the last. It is the working assumption of most religion and of most irreligion — that when the question comes, something can be said: sincerity, decency, intention, comparison with worse men. The parable removes the option. And notice the address: the king calls him Friend, the same word Christ used to Judas in the garden. Nearness is not safety, and a place at the table is not a garment.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek phimoo (G5392), to muzzle, put to silence; siopao (G4623), to be silent; eneos (G1769), speechless, dumb with amazement.

expand to see more

Greek phimoo (G5392) — to muzzle, silence; Matthew 22:12, Mark 4:39, 1 Timothy 5:18.

Greek eneos (G1769) — speechless, dumb; Acts 9:7 only.

Greek siopao (G4623) — to be silent, hold one's peace; Luke 1:20, Mark 14:61.

Greek phrasso (G5420) — to stop, close the mouth; Romans 3:19, 2 Corinthians 11:10.

Greek hupodikos (G5267) — guilty, answerable to; Romans 3:19 only.

Usage

"“And he was speechless” — the guest without a wedding garment."

"“Thou shalt be dumb… because thou believest not my words” — Gabriel to Zacharias."

"“That every mouth may be stopped” — the law's purpose, in Paul's words."
